talks.title: Implementing a Zero Knowledge Proof -
talks.summary:
### Implementation Mechanics of Zero-Knowledge Proofs
At 00:00, cryptographic researcher Cathie Yun presents a practical implementation walkthrough of the Bulletproofs zero-knowledge proving system, focusing on engineering efficient range proofs in Rust.

### Mathematical Prerequisites and Theoretical Foundations
At 07:00, Yun introduces the foundational requirements of zero-knowledge systems: completeness (an honest prover can convince the verifier), soundness (a cheating prover cannot convince the verifier), and zero-knowledge (the proof reveals nothing beyond the statement's validity).

### Prime-Order Cyclic Groups and Pedersen Commitments
At 14:01, the speaker explains the mathematical structure of Bulletproofs. Built over prime-order elliptic curve groups (such as Ristretto), the protocol leverages Pedersen commitments to commit to hidden values using blinding factors without leaking the underlying data.

### Inner-Product Arguments Without Trusted Setups
At 21:00, Yun deconstructs the inner-product argument that distinguishes Bulletproofs from other zero-knowledge architectures. Unlike zk-SNARKs, Bulletproofs require no trusted setup ceremony and achieve compact logarithmic proof sizes.

### Programmable Constraint Systems in Rust
Concluding between 28:00 and 35:00, Yun demonstrates the open-source `bulletproofs` Rust library. She illustrates how developers can build arithmetic circuits and rank-1 constraint systems (R1CS) to verify complex computational statements and enable confidential blockchain transactions.

talks.title: Migrating to quantum safe crypto -
talks.summary:
### Engineering Strategies for Post-Quantum Migration
At 00:00, Christian Paquin from Microsoft Research presents on preparing enterprise software architectures for the post-quantum cryptographic transition at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Paquin outlines the timeline and engineering hurdles facing secure communications.

### Cryptographic Agility in Enterprise Software
At 05:20, Paquin emphasizes the necessity of cryptographic agility. He explains that systems must be designed to swap cryptographic algorithms dynamically without requiring major software redesigns, drawing parallels to historical migrations from MD5 to SHA-256 and TLS version upgrades.

### Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Exchange Architectures
At 10:29, the presentation explores hybrid cryptographic protocols. By pairing classical elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) algorithms with post-quantum lattice or isogeny-based algorithms (such as SIKE or Kyber), organizations ensure communications remain secure against future quantum decryption without sacrificing current classical security guarantees.

### Tracking the NIST Post-Quantum Standardization Effort
At 15:24, Paquin reviews the status of the ongoing NIST post-quantum standardization process. He evaluates leading candidate algorithms across lattice-based, code-based, and multivariate mathematical families, detailing performance trade-offs in key size and computational latency.

### Prototyping Post-Quantum TLS with Open-Source Tooling
Concluding between 20:52 and 25:30, the speaker details open-source testing platforms, highlighting the Open Quantum Safe (OQS) project and post-quantum OpenSSL forks. He demonstrates how developers can benchmark post-quantum TLS handshakes across realistic network environments today.

talks.title: Enabling HTTPS for home network devices -
talks.teaser: Enabling HTTPS for home network devices -
talks.summary:
### Solving the Local Network HTTPS Challenge
At 00:00, computer security researcher Karl Koscher addresses the systemic lack of transport security in home networks, presenting an automated system for provisioning trusted Let's Encrypt TLS certificates to local devices.

### The Problem with Local IoT Web Interfaces
At 04:02, Koscher examines why local network devices—including routers, network-attached storage (NAS) devices, and smart home hubs—rely on unencrypted HTTP or self-signed certificates. Because local IP subnets (192.168.x.x) cannot be validated by public certificate authorities, users are trained to ignore browser security warnings.

### Automating ACME DNS-01 Validation
At 08:02, the speaker details how the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol can overcome local network constraints. By using DNS-01 challenges rather than HTTP-01 challenges, devices can prove domain control without exposing internal web servers to the public internet.

### Open-Source Architecture: tlsmy.net
At 12:00 and 16:00, Koscher introduces an open-source Python implementation running on a public service domain (`tlsmy.net`). Local devices authenticate to the service, which updates dynamic DNS TXT records to automatically fulfill Let's Encrypt validation requests and deliver trusted wildcard certificates to home devices.

### Certificate Authority Authorization and Operational Privacy
Concluding at 20:01, Koscher reviews privacy and DNS security. He explains how CAA records prevent unauthorized certificate issuance while ensuring that internal device IP addresses remain shielded within local network perimeters.

talks.title: Adversarial Fashion Sartorial Hacking -
talks.summary:
### Garment Design as a Countermeasure to Automated Surveillance
At 00:00, security researcher and fashion designer Kate Rose introduces Adversarial Fashion at the Crypto and Privacy Village, demonstrating how apparel design can subvert automated visual surveillance systems. Rose explores how computer vision networks can be tricked using wearable physical patterns.

### Mechanics of Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs)
At 13:21, Rose examines municipal surveillance architectures powered by Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs). She details how camera networks deploy optical character recognition (OCR) and object detection models (such as YOLO) to log vehicle locations across public streets, building massive geolocation databases.

### Printing Adversarial Patterns onto Textiles
At 25:14, the presentation details the creation of adversarial fabrics. By designing textile prints covered in synthetic license plate patterns that match state-level fonts and aspect ratios, the garments trigger ALPR detection algorithms, injecting junk location readings into surveillance databases to degrade tracking accuracy.

### Optical Confusion: Retroreflective and High-Contrast Materials
At 36:56, Rose discusses sartorial hacking techniques. She demonstrates how high-contrast geometric prints and infrared-reflective fabrics disrupt bounding-box detection, preventing facial recognition and pedestrian classification algorithms from properly framing subjects.

### Wearable Activism and Open-Source Counter-Surveillance
Concluding between 42:00 and 49:44, Rose advocates for open-source adversarial fashion. She encourages developers and designers to publish wearable patterns that democratize counter-surveillance tools, empowering citizens to push back against ubiquitous physical tracking.

talks.title: Ensuring Privacy through Obfuscation -
talks.summary:
### Obfuscation as Defensive Counter-Surveillance
At 00:00, identity security strategist Mike Kiser delivers a lively exploration of noise injection and data obfuscation as pragmatic countermeasures against pervasive corporate surveillance and tracking.

### The Inadequacy of Legal Privacy Frameworks
At 10:02, Kiser critiques modern privacy legislation like GDPR and CCPA. While well-intentioned, statutory rules frequently fail to protect consumer privacy as surveillance platforms deploy deceptive consent interfaces and continue harvesting behavioral telemetry.

### Empirical Noise Injection Experiments
At 20:03, the speaker details an empirical experiment where he actively injected randomized browsing noise, contradictory search queries, and automated web traffic into his personal digital accounts over several weeks.

### Poisoning Algorithmic Profiling Models
At 30:00, Kiser demonstrates how tools like AdNauseam and TrackMeNot degrade predictive analytics. By clicking every advertisement and querying contradictory topics, automated obfuscation destroys the mathematical confidence scores that tracking platforms rely on to profile consumers.

### Behavioral Disruption and Cultural Resistance
Concluding between 40:02 and 50:00, Kiser presents the results of his experiment: tracking algorithms completely lost coherence, serving disconnected, irrelevant advertisements. He frames intentional obfuscation as an empowering form of digital civil resistance against corporate surveillance monopolies.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Compelled Device Decryption and 5A -
talks.summary:
### The Fifth Amendment and Digital Device Decryption
At 00:00, Riana Pfefferkorn, Associate Director of Surveillance and Cybersecurity at the Stanford Center for Internet and Society, delivers an analysis of Fifth Amendment protections against compelled device decryption at the Crypto and Privacy Village.

### The Privilege Against Self-Incrimination in Digital Forensics
At 06:49, Pfefferkorn reviews foundational constitutional law. She explains that the Fifth Amendment protects individuals from being compelled to provide testimonial evidence that reveals the contents of their mind, distinguishing between knowledge (such as passcodes) and physical evidence.

### The Foregone Conclusion Doctrine
At 13:48, the presentation examines prosecutorial strategies to bypass Fifth Amendment protections. Pfefferkorn analyzes the "foregone conclusion" exception, explaining how prosecutors argue that if law enforcement can prove a suspect knows the passcode and owns the device, compelling entry does not violate constitutional rights.

### Legal Disparities: Biometrics vs. Alphanumeric Passcodes
At 20:39, Pfefferkorn discusses conflicting court rulings regarding biometric unlocks versus passcodes. Many jurisdictions treat fingerprints and facial recognition as non-testimonial physical characteristics that can be compelled, prompting the speaker to recommend using emergency device features (such as iOS SOS mode) to temporarily disable biometrics.

### The Future of Constitutional Protections in Cybersecurity
Concluding between 24:00 and 28:00, Pfefferkorn outlines ongoing appellate litigation. She calls on the legal and cybersecurity communities to push for updated judicial standards that recognize the intimate privacy interests stored within modern mobile devices.

talks.title: How to Integrate Privacy Legal Security -
talks.teaser: How to Integrate Privacy Legal Security -
talks.summary:
### Bridging Legal, Security, and Privacy Disciplines
At 00:00, privacy attorney Suchismita Pahi moderates a panel exploring the operational integration of legal counsel, privacy engineering, and technical information security teams.

### Dismantling Corporate Organizational Silos
At 09:02, the panelists examine the structural friction between technical security teams, corporate lawyers, and compliance officers. Misalignment regarding regulatory risk, technical debt, and privacy controls often leaves organizations vulnerable to regulatory penalties and security incidents.

### Regulatory Enforcement and FTC Consent Decrees
At 18:01, the discussion analyzes landmark regulatory enforcement actions, focusing on the Federal Trade Commission's multi-billion-dollar consent decrees against major tech platforms, illustrating how regulatory enforcement now directly dictates technical architecture.

### Frictionless User Experiences vs. Informed Consent
At 27:00, the panel examines product design trade-offs. Fintech platforms frequently streamline user onboarding by obscuring data harvesting, and the speakers discuss how engineering teams can build seamless user flows while preserving user privacy rights.

### Proactive Privacy-by-Design and Organizational Futures
Concluding between 36:02 and 45:00, the speakers advocate for proactive "privacy-by-design" threat modeling during early software development sprints. They project the growing influence of Chief Privacy Officers (CPOs) and emphasize that engineering, legal, and security must operate as integrated partners.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Facial Recognition DNA and Biometric Privacy -
talks.teaser: Facial Recognition DNA and Biometric Privacy -
talks.summary:
### The Expanding Frontier of Biometric Surveillance
At 00:00, privacy attorney Tiffany Li examines the legal and constitutional implications of facial recognition, consumer DNA databases, and biometric surveillance at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Li explores the absence of comprehensive federal protections in the United States.

### The Regulatory Void in Federal Privacy Law
At 07:00, Li analyzes state versus federal privacy protections. While states like Illinois have enacted specific legislation like the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), the lack of federal standards leaves citizens unprotected against widespread corporate biometric tracking.

### Direct-to-Consumer Genomics and Law Enforcement Searches
At 13:24, the presentation explores consumer genetic databases. Li discusses how open-source genealogy platforms (such as GEDmatch) allow law enforcement to identify criminal suspects and their relatives through familial DNA matching, bypassing traditional Fourth Amendment warrant requirements.

### Scraping Public Media for Facial Recognition Training
At 20:07, Li critiques commercial data brokers and AI companies. She examines how firms scrape billions of publicly accessible photos from social media without user consent to build facial recognition engines marketed to law enforcement agencies and private enterprises.

### Legislative Recommendations for Biometric Governance
Concluding between 24:00 and 26:47, Li outlines necessary legal reforms. She advocates for strict consent requirements for biometric collection, statutory bans on unconsented facial surveillance in public spaces, and warrant requirements for law enforcement access to genetic databases.

talks.title: MITM mixed mode butterfly key privacy attack -
talks.teaser: MITM mixed mode butterfly key privacy attack -
talks.summary:
### Cryptographic Attacks on Vehicular Butterfly Keys
At 00:00, researcher Ben Brecht presents a man-in-the-middle privacy attack targeting the Butterfly Key expansion protocol used in Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) security credentials.

### The Privacy Mandate in Connected Vehicles
At 06:00, Brecht explains the privacy challenge facing connected transportation systems. If vehicles broadcast fixed cryptographic identities, adversaries can track citizen movements; V2X architectures mitigate this by deploying thousands of short-lived pseudonymous certificates.

### Mechanics of Butterfly Key Expansion
At 12:03, the speaker details the mathematical operation of Butterfly Keys. The protocol allows a Pseudonym Certificate Authority (PCA) to expand a single master "caterpillar key" from an onboard unit into thousands of unlinkable pseudonymous public keys without learning the vehicle's true identity.

### Executing the Man-in-the-Middle Exploit
At 18:04 and 24:01, Brecht demonstrates a novel vulnerability in the key generation handshake. An active adversary positioned on the network between the vehicle and the PCA can intercept and manipulate intermediate public key parameters, injecting mathematical offsets.

### Linking Pseudonyms and Cryptographic Mitigations
Concluding at 30:01, Brecht shows that this manipulation allows the attacker to correlate and link all subsequently issued pseudonymous certificates, completely defeating the protocol's privacy protections. He concludes by proposing mutual end-to-end response encryption between the onboard unit and the PCA to neutralize the attack.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Black Mirror You are yr own privacy nightmare -
talks.teaser: Black Mirror You are yr own privacy nightmare -
talks.summary:
### The Anatomy of Personal Information Leakage
At 00:00, social engineer Cat Murdock delivers a presentation on how personal digital footprints enable account takeovers at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Murdock illustrates how oversharing on social media provides attackers with the data necessary to compromise targets.

### Mining Open Source Intelligence from Everyday Activity
At 14:06, Murdock demonstrates OSINT collection methods. By tracking public social media updates, entertainment streaming habits, and personal check-ins, attackers can easily discover answers to common security challenge questions—such as childhood pets, schools, and maternal relatives.

### Social Engineering and Customer Support Pretexts
At 28:46, the speaker walks through vishing and support desk manipulation. Armed with biographical details gathered from OSINT, attackers call telecommunications and financial customer service representatives, confidently answering identity verification questions to initiate unauthorized password resets.

### Exploiting Customer Support Verification Trees
At 41:36, Murdock analyzes support desk triage workflows. She illustrates how attackers map out service representative call scripts to exploit alternative verification channels, successfully bypassing multi-factor authentication by targeting human customer support agents.

### Personal Threat Modeling and Privacy Hygiene
Concluding between 46:00 and 50:00, Murdock provides concrete defense recommendations. She advises individuals to use randomized, non-factual answers for security questions stored in password managers, audit public social profiles, and compartmentalize digital accounts to limit exposure.
